[RA 68-1974] 15 UNUSUAL EPONYMY-DATINGS FROM MARI AND ASSYRIA by Mogens Trolle LARSEN The Old Assyrian texts from Anatolia contain a very substantial number of year-dates and these fall into two groups: there are simple datings of the type limmum PN, and there are a great many datings of the type limmum Sa qali PN; in a couple of texts we find the formula limmum 8a warki PN. In a forthcoming study of the OA eponymic system of dating I shall attempt to show that the $a qali datings were a very special kind of mu-ussa dates which were used during the first months of the year in the Assyrian colonies in Anatolia. The year eponym was appointed in the capital Assur, apparently in a ceremony which included the drawing of lots, and it was never known on beforehand who was going to give his name to the coming year. Consequently, the Assyrians in Anatolia had to receive this information by letter, and since it appears that the change of eponym took place in very late autumn it would often take several months before it was known in the colonies what name the current year had. The full form of the formula seems to have been as follows: limmum $a ina qati PN isbutu, and we may perhaps render it loosely by: “‘eponym:   he who has taken over from PN’’}. The few examples of the sa warki formula must be assumed to have the same meaning, i.e.: ‘“‘eponymy: he who (came) after PN’’. The cases that I know about do fall in months which also typically occur in Sa qdti datings. Whereas the latter formula is found only in the OA documents from Anatolia we do have a number of instances of ($a) warki datings from other sources. I shall begin with the references from Mari, found in texts which are in fact contemporary with the later OA documents; and after that I shall turn to a brief investigation of the references from the later Assyrian documents. 1. This interpretation of the sa qdti datings was first given by H. Lewy in chapter XXIV, § VII-X, Anatolia in the Old Assyrian Period, in CAH, Revised edition, vol. I, published as separate fascicle in 1965. Essentially the same translation of the formula was suggested by J. Lewy already in 1957 in OrNS 26, p. 20, n. 3. Balkan’s criticism of this rendering in AS 16, p. 173, n. 33, is well-founded with regard to the problem of trans- lating the phrase but the meaning established by J. and H, Lewy seems assured.

The Mari texts contain references to more than one calendar, of course, and in
this context we must concentrate on the documents that can be dated to the reign
of Jasmah-Adad. This period is generally referred to with the rather misleading term
“the Assyrian interregnum”, because the king was only a puppet under the power of
his father Samsi-Adad I who is seen as an Assyrian king or emperor. It is true that the
old city Assur—till this time clearly a city-state and not the center of a territorial

However, Assur did not normally function as the capital since Samsi-Adad spent
most of his time in the town of Subat-Enlil; and it is misleading to speak of a state
“Assyria” or of an “Assyrian empire” at this time since it is clear that Samsi-Adad’s
empire did not originate in and was not built upon the men and the power of the
city-state Assur.

During Jasmah-Adad’s reign in Mari the Assyrian system of year eponymies
was used on most documents in the datings!, but the month calendar of Assur was
not made use of at all. Instead we find that the “local” texts, i.e. administrative
documents which referred to the goings-on of the palace in Mari, mostly use the old
local months. These are known also from the succeeding period when Zimrilim had
ousted Jasmah-Adad from Mari and had seized his father’s throne. However, in letters
from the Jasmah-Adad period we find a different month calendar, one which cannot
at the moment, be localized and which we therefore have to call the “Samai-Adad
calendar”, It contains a number of names which were current in many of the local
month calendars of the time but we do not have evidence which enables us to establish
even the sequence of these names®,

This hybrid calendar may very well have contained further complicating
elements for it is not at all certain that the local calendar coincided with the “imperial”
one; in other words, it remains to be shown whether the eponym year of Assur began
at the same time as the local year of the traditional Mari calendar, and it must. be
kept in mind that the reconstruction of this calendar has been based upon the evidence

My interpretation of the OA data, in particular the sa qati datings, leads to the
conclusion that the eponym year did not begin with spring equinox; rather, the evidence
from level 2, the early OA period, indicates winter solstice as a likely starting point
for the new year, but in the later OA period, level Ib, one could also think of autumn
equinox. The local Mari calendar, on the other hand, appears to have followed the
normal southern pattern so that the first month of the year coincided approximately
with spring equinox. There are several indications of this, and I shall only mention
a few quite obvious ones. Thus, month XII is called ebarum, “harvest”, and that most
probably corresponds to the Sumerian Se-kin-kud, i.e. the time of the cutting of the
grain‘. Practically all loan contracts from Mari stipulate repayment in the month
abum (IV); a few instead mention payment “at harvest time on the threshing floor”.
It is accordingly clear that the harvest month (ebirum) fell in spring and that
the grain was ready for delivery in abum, i.e. in late summer’. One may also mention

It is obvious that the warki datings from the year following the eponymy of
‘Tab-silli-ASur cannot, be explained in the same way as the sa qati datings from the
colonies in Anatolia. Traffic between Assur and Mari could not possibly be cut off
during several months due to harsh weather, so the only explanation that seems to offer
itself is that the eponym in Assur was not appointed at the correct. time. Such an
omission could of course have different, causes but the simplest interpretation is that
disorders of some nature, presumably political or military, prevented the orderly
succession of eponymies. If we carry this hypothesis further we must conclude that
the texts dated to the months in the year “after ‘Tab-silli-A8’ur” stem from the last
days of Jasmah-Adad’s reign in Mari.

 

In fact, Bottéro has already mentioned this possibility since he could show that
there are more dated texts from ‘Tab-silli-ASSur’s eponymies (and especially from the
“warki-months”) than from any other eponymy®. It is logical to conclude that the
majority of the administrative documents found should stem from the last year.
Bottéro could furthermore show that ‘ab-silli-A8Sur’s eponymy followed directly
upon the eponymy of a certain Adad-bini, and this is of considerable interest since
it is very likely that this latter eponym was the last one attested from the Samsi-Adad
archives in the town at Chagar Bazar‘, In other words, the archives there stop about
1 1/2 year before the archives from Jasmah-Adad’s reign at Mari, and it is therefore
possible to envisage a slowly progressing collapse of Samsi-Adad’s empire, presumably

 

beginning in the north-west. The texts from Mari which are dated to the eponymy
after ‘Tab-silli-A&Sur may accordingly provide us with information about what
happened during the last months of Jasmah-Adad’s reign.

However, the monotonous lists of deliveries of oil and perfumes appear
to continue through these months without any change—and it may indeed be wrong
to expect these administrative texts to show any signs of the general political situation.
